comparators.name: Ch. 1: What Is Philosophy?
comparators.question: What Is Philosophy?
comparators.method: The greatest narrowing of philosophy would be to regard it merely as a history of the views of great philosophers. Philosophy is fundamentally the self-aware intellectual activity through which human beings ask for the reasons behind their beliefs, experiences, values, practices, and institutions. Philosophy brings into question what ordinary life treats as self-evident. “This is true”—why? “This is right”—by what standard?…
comparators.purvapaksha: Philosophy is only the history of ideas
comparators.uttarapaksha: A Critical Dialogue with History
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not discard history; it communicates the present on the basis of history. Don 't force the thinker of the past into the current vocabulary but examine the present relevance of their question. Philosophy thus becomes the junction of history and living reason.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 1

comparators.name: Ch. 2: Questions, Doubt, and Pramāṇa
comparators.question: Questions, Doubt, and Pramāṇa
comparators.method: Doubt is not the enemy of knowledge. disciplined doubt is the keeper of knowledge. But unfounded and equal degrees of infinite doubt about everything is not the ideal of knowledge. If we completely distrust direct perception, memory, linguistic reasoning, and our own reasoning and all shared experiences at the same time, not only philosophy but general behavior will be impossible. The basic question, therefore, is whether or…
comparators.purvapaksha: How All Evidence Will Finally Be Proven
comparators.uttarapaksha: The Beginning of Error Checking
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not seek absolute, external, or omniscient evidence. Common-sense procedures can be given preliminary authority unless there is reasonable resistance; when opposed, mutual testing, independent evidence, and practical success are used to modify the belief through rationalization and source testing. This is not infallibility, but error correctionism.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 2

comparators.name: Ch. 3: Truth and Perspective
comparators.question: Truth and Perspective
comparators.method: They are true in their own right; their sentences seem attractive to express tolerance, but philosophically call for caution. If two people say the same thing at the same time, in the same sense, the opposite is true: the lamp is burning and the lamp is not burning; both statements cannot be true in the same sense. But this hard fact does not even lead to the conclusion that every reality ends up in only one description. A…
comparators.purvapaksha: To say that truth is multifaceted would not lead to relativism.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Vision Multipleity Criteria Shared
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophy says that there can be many perspectives, but each claim must endure sound reason, internal consistency, and the resistance of available evidence, opposition, and experience. Separate statements can be complementary; the question of a decision between diametrically opposed statements cannot be avoided.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 3

comparators.name: Ch. 4: The Limits of Knowledge
comparators.question: The Limits of Knowledge
comparators.method: We all know that the person who says this is not knowledge speaks the language of arrogance. Human knowledge is limited, cognitive is limited, memory is flawed, attention is selective, language is incomplete, concepts are historical, institutions may be biased, and everyone 's experience is limited. However, this limitation does not imply that knowledge is impossible. The basic tenet of Parallel Philosophy is that knowledge…
comparators.purvapaksha: What is the strongest objection or rival explanation that this inquiry must face?
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.

comparators.name: Ch. 5: The Method of Parallel Philosophy
comparators.question: The Method of Parallel Philosophy
comparators.method: Parallelism is not another name for opposition. Parallel roads may exist alongside a main road; sometimes main roads are useful, sometimes blocked, and sometimes they are constructed so that many settlements are inaccessible. Parallel philosophy is not a project to break the mainstream; it is a method to broaden the horizons of knowledge. It aims to add missed sources, rigorously test established arguments, communicate…
comparators.purvapaksha: So many methods would kill the creativity of philosophy.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Discipline is not the enemy of creativity
comparators.synthesis: In music, the grammar of the raga makes possible the creation of uninterrupted or inverted nuances. Philosophical discipline prevents fiction from being presented as fact. Independent narration is more powerful when the reader knows where history ends and the author 's new argument begins.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 5

comparators.name: Ch. 6: Vedic Thought and Upanishadic Questions
comparators.question: Vedic Thought and Upanishadic Questions
comparators.method: It is not appropriate to read the earliest background of Indian philosophy as the history of a ready-made theory. In Vedic literature, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanishads, the rituals, deities, world-creation, speech, death, the soul, karma, knowledge, and liberation communicate with and sometimes oppose each other in multiple voices. From this plural world arises the question of later systematic philosophies.
comparators.purvapaksha: 6.16 Purvapaksha: Are the Upanishads only spiritual poems?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Forms of philosophy are not just formulaic arguments. The Upanishads systematically question the limits of existence, knowledge, the self, death, reason, value, and language; they develop arguments through dialogue and example. However, it is also wrong to make every poetic sentence a complete metaphysical theory. Philosophical reconstruction must respect the literary nature of the sources.
comparators.synthesis: Parallel to the Vedic-Upanishadic world, philosophy accepts four basic teachings. First, doubts and questions are also possible within a religious tradition. Secondly, the meaning of external rituals may be reinterpreted by internal experience. Third, multiple answers can coexist in the same tradition. Fourth, acknowledging the limits of knowledge and not abandoning it leads…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 6

comparators.name: Ch. 7: Sāṃkhya
comparators.question: Sāṃkhya
comparators.method: Samkhya is one of the most influential metaphysical systems in Indian philosophy. Its fundamental problem is how to understand the relationship between conscious experience and the changing world. Samkhya answers this question through two primordial elements: Purusha, the pure consciousness; and Prakriti, the transforming primordial nature. Salvation is possible when men know themselves to be different from the vices of…
comparators.purvapaksha: The Passive Consciousness How the Experientialistic?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Samkhya states that the inborn nature is not self-manifested; conscious witness is necessary to explain the presence of experience. The intellect transforms the content of experience: man is the condition of his light. But this answer does not completely eliminate the problem of relativity; herein lies both the philosophical strength and the difficulty of Samkhya.
comparators.synthesis: Parallel to Samkhya, philosophy takes three major methodological approaches. First, separate out the experimenter and the experience content. Secondly, analyze the complex world in a hierarchical causal structure. Third, while accepting the strong insight of a philosophical system, the difficult question of man-nature relations and polyandry should not be confused with…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 7

comparators.name: Ch. 8: Yoga
comparators.question: Yoga
comparators.method: Yoga is often presented in the modern world as a form of posture, physical flexibility, or wellness practice. This usage is not without significance, but the philosophical scope of Patanjali 's yoga philosophy is quite broad. Yoga embodies a systematic approach to the mind, to the causes of suffering, to moral discipline, to meditation, to knowledge, to action, to samadhi and to Kaivalya. The fundamental question is whether…
comparators.purvapaksha: Is Yoga an Escapism?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Classical yoga presents a primarily individualistic discipline of liberation; it should not be confused with modern social justice theory. But self-discipline, nonviolence, control of greed, and meditation can become forces for moral action. Parallel philosophy here links the internal discipline of yoga with social justice, institutional responsibility, and the analysis of material circumstances without making one a substitute for the other.
comparators.synthesis: Four lessons can be drawn from yoga: do not take mental processes for granted; practice is incomplete without thoughtful transformation; moral discipline is linked to cognitive discipline; and self-control does not replace social responsibility. There need not be an artificial opposition between individual liberty and public justice.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 8

comparators.name: Ch. 9: Nyāya
comparators.question: Nyāya
comparators.method: Nyaya philosophy is a highly developed tradition of logic, proof, argumentation, and realism in Indian intellectual history. Justice does not mean mere formal argument; it is the name of the whole discipline of proper inquiry, evidentiary judgment, and reasoned argument. The introduction to the Nyaya Sutras alludes to this broader project of discussing knowledge-sources, objects of knowledge, objects of doubt, examples,…
comparators.purvapaksha: 9.14 PrevParty: Is justice a highly technical regard
comparators.uttarapaksha: Technical language is a means of reducing ambiguity that is not possible. Criticism is appropriate if the nuanced term becomes merely a show of scholarship; however, conceptual nuance is essential when multiple meanings of the same word provoke controversy. The judicial ideal is the transparency of reason, not the worship of technicalities.
comparators.synthesis: Parallel to justice, philosophy adopts five basic disciplines: examine if in doubt. elucidate the evidence for a claim. present the opposition forcefully. find fault with the reason. and maintain sound judgment without aiming to win the argument. At the same time, this tradition can be extended to new areas by adding modern source-review and scientific methods and social…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 9

comparators.name: Ch. 10: Vaiśeṣika
comparators.question: Vaiśeṣika
comparators.method: The peculiarity of Vaisheshika is that he does not confine philosophy to the question of liberation or enlightenment, but dares to systematically classify the world into whatever kinds of entities are perceived. For this reason, Vaisheshika is a very important realist tradition in Indian metaphysics. Its core questions are why materialism is made up of basic types of objects, qualities, actions, and relationships, and how to…
comparators.purvapaksha: Previous: Why do we need to accept so many categories?
comparators.uttarapaksha: In the latter case, Vaisheshika may say that a separate category is necessary for a proper explanation of the actual differences in language and experience. I would not be able to tell the real difference if the traits and individuals considered similarities and relationships were the same kind of entity. But the number of categories is not the only convention; each category adds a criterion parallel to the other to prove its explanatory function.
comparators.synthesis: There are three main takeaways from Vaisheshika. First, the classification of reality itself is a philosophical task; categories should not be taken to be natural and self-evident. The second is the right to assume a microcosm when it has a clear explanatory role. Third, problem-structuring dialogues are more productive than drawing historical parallels with modern science.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 10

comparators.name: Ch. 11: Pūrvamīmāṃsā
comparators.question: Pūrvamīmāṃsā
comparators.method: Preliminaries are among the most important traditions of Indian philosophy, where the focus is not only on the question of what makes up the universe or what constitutes a soul but also on questions such as how humans know duty, how sentences give meaning, how evidence gains its credibility, and how rituals guide action. The Jāminika Mīmāṃsāra begins with a query to the Dharmapada. Here, dharma is not merely a general…
comparators.purvapaksha: Premise is only the act itself.
comparators.uttarapaksha: From the Interpretation of Karma to the Philosophy of Knowledge
comparators.synthesis: The philosophical value of presuppositions lies not in their acceptance of every theological conclusion, but in the fact that they subject to rigorous analysis the prescriptive language, the meaning of texts, the self-validation and refutation of evidence, and the knowledge of duty.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 11

comparators.name: Ch. 12: Vedānta
comparators.question: Vedānta
comparators.method: The literal meaning of the Vedanta text is linked to the end or Paripaka of the Vedas; however, in philosophical history, it is a broad family of many traditions centered on the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras, and the Bhagavad Gita. It would be wrong to equate Vedanta with Advaita alone. Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita, and other Vedantic schools hold serious disagreements on the relationship between Brahman and the world,…
comparators.purvapaksha: All the Vedantas ultimately say the same thing.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Dialogue is not Unity: A Disciplined Study of Plurality
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophies do not artificially unite traditions. He asks the common question of where there are real differences and what logic depends on which assumptions.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 12

comparators.name: Ch. 13: Buddhist Philosophy
comparators.question: Buddhist Philosophy
comparators.method: It would be an injustice to Buddhist philosophy 's vast philosophical tradition to confine it solely to religious precepts or the formula of nothingness. The Buddhist traditions of suffering and impermanence, of non-self and non-self, of perception and production, of karma and nirvana, of knowledge and language, of direct perception and compassion and emptiness, have all developed profound controversies over the centuries.…
comparators.purvapaksha: Buddhist philosophy is atheistic nihilism.
comparators.uttarapaksha: The Philosophy of Dependence, Process, and Liberation
comparators.synthesis: Buddhist philosophy questions the independent essence of existence, but accepts a practical world of reason, morality, and suffering. The purpose of their negative reasoning is to dispel multiple false attachments and not to establish zero atheism.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 13

comparators.name: Ch. 14: Jain Philosophy
comparators.question: Jain Philosophy
comparators.method: Jain philosophy presents the most developed traditions of nonviolence, living and nonliving, karma, anekantavada, nayavada, and samvada in Indian intellectual history. In popular parlance, Anekantavada is said to be their own true religion; however, this is a philosophically incorrect simplification. The Jain view accepts the multifacetedness of the object, and at the same time disciplines the narrative from a conditional…
comparators.purvapaksha: Anekantavada is contradictory in itself.
comparators.uttarapaksha: The Principle Itself Conditional
comparators.synthesis: The strength of the Jain tradition lies in the way Anekantavada also places its claims within the contextual analysis. That omniscience is the discipline of limited statement, not the claim of ordinary being.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 14

comparators.name: Ch. 15: Lokāyata and Materialist Questions
comparators.question: Lokāyata and Materialist Questions
comparators.method: The history of Indian philosophy is not just the history of the Vedas, the soul, salvation, and acceptance of God. There were also traditions that valued direct experience, the body and matter, and criticism of worldly life and religious claims. The term ālokayata or ālokācārava is associated with this materialist-scientific tradition. However, its study requires special source-care as the original texts are mostly…
comparators.purvapaksha: Lokāyata is the lowest or only negative aspect of Indian philosophy.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Criticism as Philosophical Contribution to Self
comparators.synthesis: The historical nature of the Lokayata is partly obscured by the materialistic and skeptical questions preserved in its name, proving the plurality of Indian philosophy. This tradition serves as a reminder that the authority of karma or scripture over the soul and the afterlife was not a unanimous conclusion in Indian history.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 15

comparators.name: Ch. 16: Language, Word, and Meaning
comparators.question: Language, Word, and Meaning
comparators.method: Language is not only a means to express ideas; many times, it also shapes ideas. Human beings understand the world through words, categories, names, relationships and sentences. For this reason, philosophy of language is not just an extension of grammar; it is central to epistemology, metaphysics, social philosophy, and ontology. How words give meaning Whether a sentence means only a combination of words A holistic…
comparators.purvapaksha: If language shapes thought, then objective truth is impossible
comparators.uttarapaksha: Language is not just a screen over the world; it is a means of connection with the world. Language affects classification and perception, but the external world resists the direct and practical linguistic demands of cross-examination and translation. Linguistic mediation produces a consciousness of the conditions for access to truth, not the impossibility of truth.
comparators.synthesis: The varnam is audible and fleeting respectively, yet conveys the unified meaning of the sentence at once. Explosion theory tries to understand the unity of this sense. The phonetic expression is interpreted as a stable linguistic unit of meaning.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 16

comparators.name: Ch. 17: Videha: A Geography of Questioning
comparators.question: Videha: A Geography of Questioning
comparators.method: The intellectual history of Mithila cannot be understood from the present-day administrative boundaries alone. The political geography of Nepal is a term of distinct historical significance, given its location in present-day Himachal Pradesh and modern-day Bihar. In ancient texts, Videha appears as a political-cultural domain; in later traditions, Mithila evolves into a philosophical, juridical, linguistic, and cultural…

comparators.question: Yājñavalkya, Gārgī, and Maitreyī
comparators.method: The dialogues of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad present both the dramatic and conceptual depth of questions in the history of Indian philosophy. Yajnavalkya is the principal orator, but it would be unfair to consider Gargi Vachaknavi and Maitreyi as mere supporting characters voicing their opinions. Their question sets out the philosophical problem itself. The parallel text reads the dialogue as a multilingual philosophical…
