comparators.name: Ch. 19: Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and Mithila’s Logical Tradition
comparators.question: Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and Mithila’s Logical Tradition
comparators.method: A discussion of the philosophical glories of Mithila would be limited to a list of acharyas. The real contribution to methodology is to clarify claims, define terms, establish counterarguments, examine the extent of evidence, identify assumptions, distinguish relationships, and support conclusions in the face of objections. The Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition and the later Navya-Nyaya present a richer version of this logical…
comparators.purvapaksha: Technological Arguments Not Far from Human Suffering and Social Justice
comparators.uttarapaksha: Logic by itself is not justice, but without a sense of justice, reason can be blind, and without reason, reason is incompatible. It is a moral duty to listen to the victim 's side of the story, because logical clarity is essential to understand the structure and solution. Parallel philosophy does not consider compassion and reason to be competing.
comparators.synthesis: The logical tradition is not sustained by the intellect of the great man alone; the school, the manuscript, and the master-disciple sequence demand the rule of patronage and debate. Evidence for this institution is to be found in the study of Mithila 's logistical rituals.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 19

comparators.name: Ch. 20: Udayanācārya
comparators.question: Udayanācārya
comparators.method: Udayanacharya is the principal philosopher of the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, whose work systematizes and refines many of the arguments of the older Nyaya-Vaisheshika. His importance lies not only in the cause of God-realisation but also in his intervention in many areas of spiritual thought and juridical metaphysics, including the soul and matter, causality, the universal, Buddhist transcendentalism, and non-spiritualism.…
comparators.purvapaksha: Udayana 's God-realization is irrelevant today
comparators.uttarapaksha: The present importance of a historical argument does not depend solely on whether its conclusions are accepted today. Udayana systematizes the questions of causality, interpretation, and the limits of inference, as well as classical evidence and the weight of counterarguments. Modern philosophers who disagree with this argument can learn from its structure.
comparators.synthesis: Udayana 's God-criticism presupposes a number of hypotheses; it would be unfair to reduce it to a single line of reasoning for wanting to create all things. The term activity and event demand a different set of commitments, based on the difference between tradition and morality.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 20

comparators.name: Ch. 21: Vācaspati Miśra
comparators.question: Vācaspati Miśra
comparators.method: Vachaspati Mishra is significant in the history of Indian philosophy not only because he expounded on texts belonging to several philosophical traditions. His importance lies in the fact that his work makes it abundantly clear that Indian philosophy was not a collection of closed cells cut across generations, but a world of constant cross-referencing, debate, and reinterpretation. For parallel philosophy, Vachaspati Mishra is…
comparators.purvapaksha: Multiculturalism leads to a weakening of philosophical commitment
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 21

comparators.name: Ch. 22: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya
comparators.question: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya
comparators.method: Gangesh Upadhyaya 's Tattvacintamani represents a turning point in the history of Indian ontology. The text 's four broad sections, namely the direct inference, analogy, and terminology, elevate judicial evidentiary theory to a level of meticulous analysis that formed the basis for the language and methodology of later neoliberal traditions. Modern research considers Gangesh to be an early central figure in the…
comparators.purvapaksha: Excessive subtlety cuts philosophy out of life
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 22

comparators.name: Ch. 23: Navya-Nyāya: The Subtle Discipline of Language
comparators.question: Navya-Nyāya: The Subtle Discipline of Language
comparators.method: Neo-Nyaya is not merely a new school in Indian philosophy but the development of a distinct language and method of philosophical analysis. In this tradition, after Gangesha Upadhyaya, the relationship of concepts was expressed with such subtlety that it became a style of technical analysis distinct from the usual Sanskrit philosophical prose.
comparators.purvapaksha: Excessive analysis destroys the complexity of real life
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 23

comparators.name: Ch. 24: Folk Tradition, Śāstra, and Parallel Mithila
comparators.question: Folk Tradition, Śāstra, and Parallel Mithila
comparators.method: The philosophy of Mithila is not limited to Sanskrit texts, formal treatises, or eminent acharyas. Folklore, storytelling, stories, rituals, festivals, advertisements, agricultural life, women 's experiences, family relationships, and riverine landscape practices all embody the value of human life, time, the relationship between body and nature, and notions of justice. It is not appropriate to declare these materials without…
comparators.purvapaksha: To call folk material philosophy is to exaggerate the extent of
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Mithila's parallel tradition · Chapter 24

comparators.name: Ch. 25: Greek Questions
comparators.question: Greek Questions
comparators.method: Ancient Greek philosophy occupies a central place in the history of Western philosophy, but it is historically inaccurate to regard it as the only beginning of human thought. Serious ideas about nature, order, morality, death, the kingdom, and knowledge also developed in India, China, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and other civilizations. The uniqueness of Greek philosophy should be sought in its questioning, treatise-tradition and…
comparators.purvapaksha: The history of Western philosophy would be obscured if Greek philosophy were removed from the center
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 25

comparators.name: Ch. 26: Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle
comparators.question: Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle
comparators.method: With Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, ancient Greek philosophy enters a new phase. The question of the essence of nature now joins man to the question of knowledge, virtue, justice, the state, education, the soul, and the good life. It is easy to tie these three philosophers together, but not necessarily. Socrates ' ideas are preserved mainly in the form of dialogues and questions.Plato develops the forms of justice, knowledge,…
comparators.purvapaksha: Why We Must Examine the Great Texts in a Modern Moral Test
comparators.uttarapaksha: It is necessary to understand the historical context but not prohibited by moral judgments. We can understand why an idea was possible in its day and at the same time ask whether its arguments are acceptable today. Historical understanding and ethical criticism are not mutually exclusive.
comparators.synthesis: Socrates Ignorance means not knowing anything about everything. This means recognizing the limits of one 's claim and not assuming prestige or majority or self-confidence to be evidence of knowledge. In dialogue, the question subtly shows that the initial definition does not tolerate exceptions: examples conflict with one another, or the speaker is unconsciously assuming two…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 26

comparators.name: Ch. 27: Medieval Philosophy
comparators.question: Medieval Philosophy
comparators.method: The term Middle Ages itself is a special European time division. Applying this mechanically to the history of the entire world leads to confusion. During the Middle Ages in Europe, India, the Islamic world, Jewish intellectual centres, China and other regions underwent distinct historical chronologies and philosophical transformations. Thus, in this chapter, medieval philosophy is used primarily in the context of European,…
comparators.purvapaksha: Medieval philosophy was nothing but theology.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Religious questions predominated, but logic, language, existence, causation, knowledge, morality, and questions of politics and law received independent philosophical analysis. The boundaries of theology and philosophy are not always clear, but to call it non-philosophical is historically incorrect.
comparators.synthesis: To call medieval philosophy simply the suppression of reason by faith erases historical diversity. Some thinkers consider logic to be an explanation of religious truth, some distinguish claims based on verifiable inferences and revelations from natural intelligence, and others emphasize the limitations of logic. Belief and intellect are not two fixed camps; they are names of…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 27

comparators.name: Ch. 28: Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz
comparators.question: Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz
comparators.method: In seventeenth-century Europe, the question of the basis of certain knowledge intensified amid science and mathematics, crusades and political changes, and the transformation of the institutions of knowledge. Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz are often referred to as the intellectuals. This classification is useful for study, but the ideas of the three philosophers are not identical.
comparators.purvapaksha: The pursuit of a certain knowledge is an impossible ideal
comparators.uttarapaksha: Absolute infallibility is not possible, but clarity and the ideal of cross-examination are valuable. The problem lies in making infallibility a necessary condition of knowledge. Parallel philosophy tends to favor error correction knowledge.
comparators.synthesis: Descartes 's skepticism is a method of finding a definitive basis for not permanently abandoning all belief systems in life. The senses sometimes give off illusions; dream experiences seem to awaken - and systematic deception in thought may be considered possible. But nothing is certain: the findings themselves are an act of skepticism.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 28

comparators.name: Ch. 29: Locke, Berkeley, and Hume
comparators.question: Locke, Berkeley, and Hume
comparators.method: Locke, Berkeley and Hume are often considered the three principal names of the British empiricist tradition. They find common ground in the importance of the initial content of empirical knowledge, but their conclusions about the causality of matter and spirit in the external world and the limits of knowledge are very different.
comparators.purvapaksha: Empiricism itself may be considered a theory outside of experience.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Empiricism is not a single rigid formula. The differences between Locke, Berkeley, and Hume show that the meaning of experience is itself a broader dispute over the role of the mind and the place of reason.
comparators.synthesis: Locke regards experience as the source of knowledge, but the mind is not merely a passive storehouse. Sensing gives content from external objects, introspection gives insight into the mind 's own actions, and the mind forms complex ideas through comparison, combination, and abstraction. Criticism of innate ideas is not to deny the organization of experience.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 29

comparators.name: Ch. 30: Kant
comparators.question: Kant
comparators.method: Immanuel Kant is the turning point in modern philosophy where the previous controversies of rationalism and empiricism are renewed. Their question is how is the experience possible? The Limits of the Level of Knowledge What is the basis of a moral duty? How it is possible to make an aesthetic decision How can a human being think independently?
comparators.purvapaksha: Kant 's universal morality is highly abstract.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Criticism is appropriate, but universality itself is not. Without universal dignity, powerful groups can make their own special rules. What is needed is a solid analysis of the universal moral criterion + historical inequality.
comparators.synthesis: Kant 's fundamental question is how it is possible to have knowledge that enhances experience, but not merely generalizes specific experiences. Some basic decisions in mathematics and the natural sciences are examples of synthetic precedents for them. While adding new things to the subject of empirical methods, these empirical methods do not derive their necessary…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 30

comparators.name: Ch. 31: Hegel and Dialectic
comparators.question: Hegel and Dialectic
comparators.method: Hegel 's philosophy is an ambitious attempt to understand history, consciousness, society and reason in the same dynamic process in modern European thought. The fundamental strength of his philosophy lay in the idea that reality should not be thought of as a mere collection of static objects. Human beings, institutions, ideas, ethics and history are built within these shifting relationships. Resistance is not only a barrier…
comparators.purvapaksha: There are many forms of opposition, transformation, and argument in Indian philosophy, but to call them precursors to Hegelian conflict would be anachronistic. The jurisprudential Purvapaksha, Purvottara Paksha, the Buddhist Madhyamaka pratipada-vibhagana, Samkhya 's qualitative changes, and Vedantic differences are all distinct historical approaches to debate. Useful comparisons are here so that truth-finding does not remove the opposition but makes it a means of reflection. Mithila 's shastrartha-samskara also develops the discipline of listening to the opposing side.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Opposition is real, results are out
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophy accepts the reality of opposition but does not consider the outcome to be predetermined. A single protest can lead to reform, repression, dissolution, compromise or violence. Human actions, institutions, chance, technology, resources and moral choices influence the course of history.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 31

comparators.name: Ch. 32: Marx
comparators.question: Marx
comparators.method: Marx brings labour and production, property, class and material social relations to the centre of modern philosophy. His question is: What role does the economic and social structure play in shaping the institutions that humans think in and the moral language they use? If philosophy remained only within consciousness and did not look at factories, wages, land relations, property and division of labour, the real power…
comparators.purvapaksha: Explains the Basics of Economics
comparators.uttarapaksha: The cause is multifactorial.
comparators.synthesis: Economic structures are influential, but social histories have overlapping causes. Religious institutions may change the property structure. caste may limit the labour market. laws may change the distribution of property. language may influence educational opportunities. Parallel philosophy expands economic analysis, not abolishes it.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 32

comparators.name: Ch. 33: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche
comparators.question: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche
comparators.method: In nineteenth-century European philosophy, Kierkegaard and Nietzsche both sharpened the question of the individual 's life choices, values, and self-relationship against the larger system, though both take very different approaches. Kierkegaard emphasizes individual concerns and decisions, faith and existential responsibility; Nietzsche questions the origin of values, the genealogical power of morality, self-formation and…
comparators.purvapaksha: What is the strongest objection or rival explanation that this inquiry must face?
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 33

comparators.name: Ch. 34: Phenomenology and Existentialism
comparators.question: Phenomenology and Existentialism
comparators.method: Phenomenalism tries to understand experience in the form it appears in consciousness. Existentialism sharpens within this experience questions of freedom, choice, death, anxiety, futility, responsibility, and authentic life. The two traditions are not to be confused, but there is a deep dialogue between them in many twentieth-century thinkers.
comparators.purvapaksha: What is the strongest objection or rival explanation that this inquiry must face?
comparators.uttarapaksha: The chapter answers through source criticism, comparison, and limits on the claim.
comparators.synthesis: The parallel conclusion preserves genuine disagreement while requiring shared standards of evidence, dignity, and revisability.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 34

comparators.name: Ch. 35: Analytic Philosophy
comparators.question: Analytic Philosophy
comparators.method: Analytical philosophy is not a single theory but a broad name for a number of schools of thought in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries that emphasize language, logic, knowledge, science, and the microscopic analysis of mind and concepts. Frege, Russell, Moore, Wittgenstein and many later thinkers developed different directions in this tradition. This is of particular importance for parallel philosophies because the…
comparators.purvapaksha: Premise: Clarity is the highest quality of philosophy.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Clarity is Necessary and Not Enough
comparators.synthesis: A flagrant injustice can also be an injustice. A repressive rule may be logically absolutely clear. Philosophy, therefore, must combine truth with evidence, history with morality and authority with clarity.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 35

comparators.name: Ch. 36: Pragmatism
comparators.question: Pragmatism
comparators.method: The fundamental strength of pragmatism is that it does not allow philosophy to become a mere abstract definitional game, cut off from life. In this tradition associated with Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, the relationship between thought, meaning, truth, exploration, experience, and action is repeatedly brought up. But to call pragmatism the truth that it is useful would be to trivialize its serious…
comparators.purvapaksha: If the outcome is important, what is the independent value of the theory?
comparators.uttarapaksha: The theory gives directions and the results test them. Only theory without results can become opportunism. only theory without results - rigid dogmatism.
comparators.synthesis: Peirce emphasizes genuine skepticism rather than artificial consensus. Beliefs form habits of action.Investigation begins when experience or opposing factors destabilize these habits. We are only skeptical if we say that not changing one 's behavior or decisions can be philosophical posturing.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 36

comparators.name: Ch. 37: Philosophy of Science
comparators.question: Philosophy of Science
comparators.method: Science is not just a list of facts. Science is a complex process of questioning, hypothesizing, observing, measuring, experimenting, calculating, modelling, theorizing, reproducing and institutionalizing inquiry. Scientific knowledge changes, but changes do not prove arbitrariness. In fact, the capacity for revision is the strength of science.
comparators.purvapaksha: Science has changed, so why rely on science today?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Changing can be a sign of improvement not failure. Reliability is built from the ability to perform tests, independent reviews, and revisions, rather than from infallibility.
comparators.synthesis: Scientific theories do not simply summarize observed phenomena; they propose causes or structures, predict new outcomes, and sometimes enable interventions. These three functions are not the same. A model may give correct predictions but may misinterpret the reasons.A historical science may give strong explanations without precise control.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Western philosophical traditions · Chapter 37

comparators.name: Ch. 38: The Individual and Society
comparators.question: The Individual and Society
comparators.method: A person is not born outside of society. Language and name, relationships, memory, education, business opportunities, fears, beliefs, and restrictions are all connected to the social world. But individuals are also not passive products of society. Individuals question, rebel, create new languages, reform traditions, and change institutions. The relationship between the individual and society is therefore not one-sided…
comparators.purvapaksha: The individual is a product of society, so individual responsibility is diminished.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Social causes refer to responsibilities and do not eliminate them completely. Responsibilities should be judged on ability, compulsion, and level of knowledge and choice.
comparators.synthesis: To think of society as a sum of individuals, languages, currencies, laws, and traditions - facts that do not arise or cease at the whim of any one individual - is difficult. Conversely, if society were considered a free organism, individual suffering and responsibility would disappear. Proper analysis assumes emergent structures: those formed by the individual 's actions but…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 38

comparators.name: Ch. 39: The Justification of the State
comparators.question: The Justification of the State
comparators.method: The state orders, levies taxes, makes laws, imposes penalties, controls property, establishes borders, and sometimes uses force. For this reason, the fundamental philosophical question of the state is why this coercive power is justified. The state is there, so don 't take it as an excuse. Power and legitimacy are two different things.
comparators.purvapaksha: Without a strong kingdom, the system will fall apart.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Strong institutions are needed, not uncontrolled states. The greater the power, the greater the need for scrutiny and accountability.
comparators.synthesis: The state possesses extensive data collection expertise and coordination, but lacks the granular knowledge of local life. The Centre 's policies may fail to capture the imagination of the average person across diverse geographies and languages. The capacity of the state and ignorance must be acknowledged at the same time.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 39

comparators.name: Ch. 40: Freedom
comparators.question: Freedom
comparators.method: Freedom does not mean the state alone cannot stop me. Individuals may be legally free, without real options due to hunger, debt, caste exclusion, patriarchy, illiteracy, violence, lack of disability-friendly structures, or societal fears. At the same time, freedom is destroyed again when the state or community takes over the choice of the individual in the name of real freedom. Freedom is therefore a concept with many layers.
comparators.purvapaksha: Creating this level of freedom does not make the concept too broad.
comparators.uttarapaksha: It is important to have a level head. Oppression-indifference is not the same thing as ability and autonomy, but all three are important for understanding true human freedom. The analysis should make it clear what level is being discussed.
comparators.synthesis: Having many options does not automatically mean more freedom. The numbers give an illusion when all options are insecure, abusive or financially impossible. A reliable exit would sometimes be worth more than ten hypothetical options.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 40

comparators.name: Ch. 41: Equality
comparators.question: Equality
comparators.method: Equality does not mean making all human beings uniform. It is fundamentally equality of moral status: every person possesses equal basic dignity, equal civic respect, and an equal claim to public justification. Modern political philosophy then raises a difficult question: equality of what—rights, opportunities, resources, capabilities, respect, or political influence? Without answering this question, “equality” can become a…
comparators.purvapaksha: Natural Differences Because Inequality is Natural
comparators.uttarapaksha: Natural differences are not automatic justifications for social subordination. The difference between power, intelligence, wealth, or birth does not destroy one 's equal moral status.
comparators.synthesis: A person may work hard, but talent, family, health, birthplace, and historical occasion are not their choices. Accepting the role of effort in success, it is difficult to regard all results as having a purely moral merit. It is also unfair to call failure a character flaw.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 41

comparators.name: Ch. 42: Justice
comparators.question: Justice
comparators.method: It is not just about dispensing justice. Honor is also justice. There is also the matter of representation. They will also be able to listen in. There is also the issue of due process. Also a correction of the injustices of history. Justice asks who gets what, why, how to make decisions, how to make rules and bear the burden of rules.
comparators.purvapaksha: Justice is only applying the same rules
comparators.uttarapaksha: Uniform rules are necessary, but if the initial conditions are structurally unequal, uniformity of rules can secure long-standing unfairness in the outcome.
comparators.synthesis: People often say that a worthy person will receive his fruits. But what is merit based on: effort, contribution, necessity, sacrifice, or discipline? This criterion gives a different result. It is hard to complete the same distributions all at once.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 42

comparators.name: Ch. 43: Caste and Social Hierarchy
comparators.question: Caste and Social Hierarchy
comparators.method: Caste is not just a personal prejudice but a historical social construct. Caste long determined opportunities in marriage, labour, education, status, residence, religious rights, and social interaction. The question of caste-philosophy, therefore, is not merely a question of whether or not people like each other but of the relationship between birth and moral status.
comparators.purvapaksha: Caste is only a cultural identity
comparators.uttarapaksha: Where identity is voluntary and of equal dignity, the problem is less.But if there is inborn confinement, humiliation, exclusion and opportunism, the culture is not free from moral criticism.
comparators.synthesis: Sanitation, ritual purification and social untouchability are different concepts. Hygiene of disease-prevention asking for empirical reasons. ritual purification meaning of community. inborn impurities of man. direct opposition to equal dignity. Calling all three the same avoids discrimination in the language of health or religion.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 43

comparators.name: Ch. 44: Class and Economic Power
comparators.question: Class and Economic Power
comparators.method: Property does not just create private convenience; it also creates power. Those who control resources, land, capital, information or technology, have an influence on social decisions. The question of economic philosophy is not merely one of the quantity of money but of control and dependence, of bargaining power and democratic equality.
comparators.purvapaksha: Market Results Are Automatically Justified
comparators.uttarapaksha: Markets can be useful coordination mechanisms, but initial wealth, power, information, monopoly and external influence justice raises questions. Exchange is not automatically a proof of justice.
comparators.synthesis: Market-wage implies demand-supply and not moral sufficiency. Contracts are formal, voluntary and not dignified if full-time employment but also food, housing, health, and education is impossible.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 44

comparators.name: Ch. 45: Women, Gender, and Power
comparators.question: Women, Gender, and Power
comparators.method: In philosophical history, the word man became synonymous with the experience of men in practice several times. Control over a woman 's body, labour, reproduction, property, education and public appearance must be considered philosophical questions. Feminist philosophy does not have a uniform creed; liberal, socialist, radical, postcolonial, Dalit, intersectional and many other strands raise different questions.
comparators.purvapaksha: Equal rights were given, so gender justice was achieved
comparators.uttarapaksha: Equal rights are essential achievements, but real equality may be imperfect because of inequalities in domestic labour, violence, social expectations, resources, security and representation.
comparators.synthesis: Traditional politics may regard the home as private and the state-market as public. But within the home, labour-distribution, education, property and violence make up public capacity. Privacy can protect inequality by keeping it out of the law.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 45

comparators.name: Ch. 46: Language, Region, and Identity
comparators.question: Language, Region, and Identity
comparators.method: The language is more of a medium of communication. The language has a unique way of looking at history, memory, humor, love, folklore, religious experiences, labor terminology, family relationships, and the world. For this reason, the question of language is not only a question of grammar; it is also a question of dignity and access, of representation and structure.
comparators.purvapaksha: Division leads to linguistic rights
comparators.uttarapaksha: Equal rights not division | Humiliation and forced assimilation can lead to division Common citizenship is strengthened when multiple identities are preserved.
comparators.synthesis: Language is also a medium of knowledge and power. A proper form of linguistic pride is the creation of high-quality knowledge in one 's own language, translation, education, and increased public outreach; not the denigration of another language or community.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 46

comparators.name: Ch. 47: Democracy
comparators.question: Democracy
comparators.method: Democracy is not just about elections. If elections are held but critics remain fearful, if parliament is there but institutions are ineffective, if majority is there then minority rights are insecure, if constitution is there but social relations survive on humiliation then democracy is incomplete.
comparators.purvapaksha: Stronger, less-regulated government is better for efficient governance
comparators.uttarapaksha: Immediate motion cannot replace long-term legality and rights-protection and error-correction. Democracy may be slow, but its capacity for self-improvement depends on institutional critique.
comparators.synthesis: Elections renew the regime 's authorization from time to time, but decisions are made continuously in the intervening period. Responsibility is weakened when the citizen 's role is limited to one vote in five years.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 47

comparators.name: Ch. 48: Gandhi
comparators.question: Gandhi
comparators.method: In Gandhi 's philosophy, the relationship between truth, non-violence, satyagraha, and Swaraj, self-restraint and resourcefulness is central. They must be studied critically, not in the simplistic binary of worship or refutation. Gandhi Heritage Portal preserves original texts like * Hind Swaraj: * Satyagraha in South Africa: * Constructive Programme: * It is more appropriate to read Gandhi-Thought on the basis of these texts.
comparators.purvapaksha: Gandhi is a moral idealist, inadequate to modern structural injustice.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Criticism is powerful where appropriate, especially in questions of caste, industrialisation, and institutionalisation. But their questions of resourcefulness, non-violent resistance, self-restraint, and political morality are still important.
comparators.synthesis: The satyagrahi possesses the moral strength to awaken the conscience of the opponent by taking risks with his body. But self-pity can sometimes become emotional pressure, especially when followers take risks with leadership commands. Volunteering and information is a must.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 48

comparators.name: Ch. 49: Ambedkar
comparators.question: Ambedkar
comparators.method: At the heart of Ambedkar 's philosophy are social democracy, caste-free constitutionalism, representation, liberty, equality and fraternity. His writing considers social stigmatization as an institutional problem rather than just a moral evil.
comparators.purvapaksha: Constitutional rights do not automatically change social behaviour.
comparators.uttarapaksha: True. the law is not enough. But without laws, representation, and institutional rights, social moral change can be weak. Both law and social order are necessary for justice to prevail.
comparators.synthesis: Some reforms may reduce the harshness of discrimination, but the basic structure survives if caste group-border intermarriage and status persist. Abolition is not merely a change of heart; it is a question of social reconstruction.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Socio-political thought · Chapter 49

comparators.name: Ch. 50: What Is Religion?
comparators.question: What Is Religion?
comparators.method: It is difficult to bind religion within a single definition. Belief? Ritual? Ethics? Community? A path to liberation? Sacred experience? A way of life? Each tradition combines these elements in different proportions. The first task of philosophy of religion, therefore, is to acknowledge the plurality of the word “dharma.”
comparators.purvapaksha: To argue about religion is to insult faith.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Freedom of belief is respectable.But when religious claims affect public obligation, education, law, property or the rights of another person, public cause is necessary. The question is not one of humiliation, but of coexistence.
comparators.synthesis: Religion is neither entirely private nor entirely state. Its moral force and oppressive potential are both reflected in history. Conscientious pluralism is an attempt to preserve both freedom of religion and human dignity.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 50

comparators.name: Ch. 51: The Question of God
comparators.question: The Question of God
comparators.method: The question of God is one of the oldest and most enduring questions in philosophy. But whether there is a God is not the only question. It is first necessary to explain what is meant by God. The Creator The omniscient and omnipotent moral being The Reason for the World The Absolute Reality of the Absolute Nullity of Brahman A personal tribute to the or the symbolic center of religious experience. Different traditions take…
comparators.purvapaksha: The Question of God Eliminated from Science
comparators.uttarapaksha: The level of the question is different.
comparators.synthesis: With the progress of logic and science, the gods of certain realms become weaker. But the philosophical question of God touches not only on what physical processes produce phenomena but also on questions of existence, causality, value, consciousness, and ultimate interpretation. Just because something is a philosophical question does not make God perfect. Science and…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 51

comparators.name: Ch. 52: Faith and Reason
comparators.question: Faith and Reason
comparators.method: The inevitable enemies of faith and reason greatly narrow the history of human theology. Some religious traditions explain doctrines through logic, while others emphasize mystery, trust, and practice or revelation. Problems arise when faith assumes itself above all criticism or when reason, forgetting its limits, declares every meaning of human experience to be meaningless.
comparators.purvapaksha: To demand proof of faith destroys the meaning of faith.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Not all faiths ask for the same kind of evidence, but public claims do ask for accountability. Personal beliefs and public truth-telling are different. The wider the impact, the clearer the justification needed.
comparators.synthesis: Failure to support the statement and proving the statement is false are different situations. However, if the claim is true, conclusive evidence is expected, and if it is not found after an exhaustive search, the absence may constitute negative evidence.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 52

comparators.name: Ch. 53: The Problem of Suffering and Evil
comparators.question: The Problem of Suffering and Evil
comparators.method: If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good, then why is there innocent suffering? It is one of the most difficult questions in philosophy. But the problem of evil is not just an intellectual conundrum. Disease, famine, violence, child-mortality, war, natural calamities and humiliation are the real sufferings. For this reason, the moral style of the philosophical answer is also important.
comparators.purvapaksha: Suffering is conclusive evidence against God
comparators.uttarapaksha: Suffering is one of the gravest challenges to theism, but for a decisive conclusion it is necessary to examine arguments concerning the probable cause of God, freedom, natural law and the limits of human knowledge. On the contrary, the problem cannot be eliminated by simply saying it is God 's plan.
comparators.synthesis: Whether the problem of evil is only suffering or not is relevant in so many ways, at so many times, and in so many senseless ways. Character can be created with little difficulty, but it is difficult to justify the extreme suffering of a child or animal with identical answers.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 53

comparators.name: Ch. 54: Karma, Rebirth, and Mokṣa
comparators.question: Karma, Rebirth, and Mokṣa
comparators.method: Karma, reincarnation, and moksha are interrelated but not synonymous concepts in many traditions of Indian philosophy. The Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions differ profoundly on the nature of karma, the continuity of karta and rebirth, and the meaning of mukti. Therefore, it is not appropriate to present the same version of the Indian karma-principle text.
comparators.purvapaksha: Karma Gives the Fullest Explanation of Moral Justice
comparators.uttarapaksha: Karma theory may be a serious form of understanding moral causality, but it is inappropriate to posit without evidence specific causes of suffering. Independent study of the natural, social, biological, and historical causes is necessary.
comparators.synthesis: If the present state is determined by past actions, what is the meaning of new actions and moral efforts? Most karma-views are not absolute determinism; rather, existing actions can give new directions by creating pre-causal circumstances.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 54

comparators.name: Ch. 55: Religious Plurality
comparators.question: Religious Plurality
comparators.method: In the same world, there exist many religious traditions, many God-concepts, many paths to liberation, and many atheistic traditions. Secularism is not only a social fact; it is also an epistemological and moral question. If intelligent, honest, and studious individuals reach conflicting religious conclusions, what effect does this have on the certainty of their beliefs?
comparators.purvapaksha: Religious Plurality Undermines the Question of Truth
comparators.uttarapaksha: Plurality does not make truth meaningless; it increases the burden of proof of a claim. The more serious the disagreement, the more obvious reasons are for politeness and cross-examination.
comparators.synthesis: The simple equivalence of God as Dharma as liberation and sin as nirvana or grace can give rise to confusion. The first act of communication is to clarify the traditional function of the word. There may be different questions behind the same words and common problems behind different words.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 55

comparators.name: Ch. 56: Religion and the State
comparators.question: Religion and the State
comparators.method: The question of the relationship between religion and the state is not as simple as simply whether the state is religious or secular. The fundamental problem in a multi-religious society is whether the legitimacy of the state rests on the equal political status of all citizens or on the privilege of claiming a religious truth. Parallel philosophies do not command the state to be heretical; they do not give the state the right…
comparators.purvapaksha: Religion is the main source of public morality. the state would be worthless without it.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Religious ethical traditions can enrich public life; but the legitimacy of the state must rest on the equal status of all citizens, not on the merit of one religion. Religious individuals are able to give public reasons. a secular state is not an anti-religious state.
comparators.synthesis: Community personal laws may protect identity and autonomy, but may affect members ' equal rights in marriage, inheritance, or guardianship. Uniformity of state can also impose a majority norm.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 56

comparators.name: Ch. 57: Folk Religion and Institutional Religion
comparators.question: Folk Religion and Institutional Religion
comparators.method: Religious life is not confined to scriptures, monasteries, temples, mosques, churches, guilds or formal doctrines. In folk life, festivals, songs, stories, fasts, household rituals, local deities, rivers, trees, ancestors, seasons, diseases, cures, agriculture, and rites of passage have religious connotations. To dismiss this world as unscriptural would be to lose sight of a vast body of religious history. But it is also…
comparators.purvapaksha: Institutional religion is corrupt. the real religion is in the people.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Public religion is not powerlessness and institutions are not just corruption. The question is not about people or institutions; the question is about how structures affect human dignity, meaning, memory, and freedom.
comparators.synthesis: The folk tales and songs may change a bit in each performance. These errors are not the only ones; new situations and experiences of listeners and speakers change the meaning. It is useful to find the original text, but not to think of the surviving versions as corrupted copies.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Religion, reason and plurality · Chapter 57

comparators.name: Ch. 58: Modernity
comparators.question: Modernity
comparators.method: Modernism is not just a term for time. Science, industry, capitalism, nation-state, individualism, bureaucracy, democracy, mass education, colonialism, markets, printing, urbanization, and new communication systems are its different historical dimensions. It is difficult to make modernity the same source or the same value story.
comparators.purvapaksha: Modernity breaks traditional bonds and frees man; therefore, their critique is reactionary.
comparators.uttarapaksha: The achievement of modern freedoms is important, but the power structure of modern institutions is not immune to criticism. Parallel philosophies choose between the knowledge of tradition without the injustice of tradition or the freedom of modernity without the dehumanization of modernity.
comparators.synthesis: Printing, assemblies, journals, and modern communication give private individuals a platform to argue public questions. But access may be limited by education, language, property, and gender; so-called public opinion may in fact be the opinion of a narrow group.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 58

comparators.name: Ch. 59: Science and the Human Being
comparators.question: Science and the Human Being
comparators.method: Science is one of the most powerful systems of knowledge in human history. Modern medicine was profoundly changed by communication, agriculture, energy, transportation, physics, and cosmology. But the power of scientific knowledge does not automatically give moral direction. What is possible and what should be done are different questions.
comparators.purvapaksha: Ethics is up to the individual. Science is only objective, so ethics must decide.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Science provides disciplined knowledge of objective facts; however, questions such as " What are the risks? " and " What are the rights? " demand a moral-political justification.
comparators.synthesis: If the results of a study are not reproducible by an independent team, the cause may be deception. Smaller samples may be due to selection bias, imprecise methods, or statistical randomness.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 59

comparators.name: Ch. 60: Language and Power
comparators.question: Language and Power
comparators.method: Language is not only the naming of ready-made realities but also the means to classify social realities, visible and invisible. The names they give sometimes affect what society considers normal, deviant, criminal, or disease rights or identities. But this fact does not lead to the conclusion that reality is created only by language. The relationship between language and the world is a complex field of existence, experience,…
comparators.purvapaksha: Language only expresses ideas. entity is outside the language.
comparators.uttarapaksha: Physical entities and institutions and resources exist outside of language, but language shapes their legitimacy, classification, and visibility. Words are not everything, but words are not useless either.
comparators.synthesis: The dictionary gives guidance on spelling and meaning while recording usage. But editorial decisions about whose text to compile, whose dialect to standardise, and how to mark off offensive meanings hold the key.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 60

comparators.name: Ch. 61: History and Memory
comparators.question: History and Memory
comparators.method: History is not just a list of what happened. History is a source selection, a question of record, an explanation, a study in silence. Not all evidence of what happened survives the same way. Royal court documents may be preserved, but not the experiences of agricultural labourers. Male genealogies may be written down. Female labours may remain in oral memory. Edicts of victors may be found in archives. The sufferings of…
comparators.purvapaksha: Adding a memory will not make the history subjective
comparators.uttarapaksha: Memory addition does not make history arbitrary if the evidence and uncertainties surrounding the source-form or transmission of memory are kept clear. Subjective experience may be one dimension of historical fact. not the only dimension.
comparators.synthesis: Listing event after event will not give a reason. Direct judgment for cause, long form, opportunity, thought and chance events should be examined separately. One reason is that it is rare enough.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 61

comparators.name: Ch. 62: Knowledge and the Digital World
comparators.question: Knowledge and the Digital World
comparators.method: In the digital world, information is abundant, knowledge is not automatic. A lie repeated a thousand times can become popular and not true. Algorithms choose attention. visual editing appears direct-jokingly. unsourced statements can reach millions. thousands of copies of the same original post can create independent confirmation-jokers confusion. Under these conditions, epistemology ceased to be merely a university subject…
comparators.purvapaksha: In the digital age, the truth has become impossible.
comparators.uttarapaksha: It is difficult, but not impossible. When fraud occurs, source-review, independent verification, archiving, and institutional transparency are all more important. A crisis of evidence is not a justification for lack of evidence.
comparators.synthesis: The first page of search results can become the limit of people 's knowledge. The ranking is made up of popularity, payouts, personal history, or platform predictions, not facts. What is not visible is out of public memory.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 62

comparators.name: Ch. 63: Artificial Intelligence and Human Responsibility
comparators.question: Artificial Intelligence and Human Responsibility
comparators.method: Artificial intelligence is the newest tool for computation, language, graphics, decision-making and knowledge organization. But because machines generate answers, moral responsibility does not automatically shift to machines. The basic question is what kind of data The Prejudice of Someone Who is the target? If a mistake is made, the person responsible for What areas of human decision making are not capable of full…
comparators.purvapaksha: If AI makes better decisions than humans, why aren 't human reviews unnecessary?
comparators.uttarapaksha: On what criteria is the best choice? Average accuracy is important, but rights, appeal, rare circumstances, price-trigger, and liability are separate questions. High performance is not absolute proof of moral legitimacy.
comparators.synthesis: The system puts the person into a risk, ability, or priority category. If there was a degree of probability, the authorities would have accepted that as a definite fact. Misclassification can have serious consequences for creditworthiness or independence.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 63

comparators.name: Ch. 64: The Environment and Future Generations
comparators.question: The Environment and Future Generations
comparators.method: Traditional morality focused mainly on the relationships between humans in the present. But the environmental crisis changes the question. I have a responsibility to the unborn generation The species is only a means for human use. The value of the river is only the market-value The decisions we make today have consequences that affect life hundreds of years from now.
comparators.purvapaksha: What are the rights of future generations when they no longer exist?
comparators.uttarapaksha: The philosophical language of entitlement may be contested, but at least it is clear that the present generation does not have unlimited permission to inflict irreversible damage that would destroy the basic life-conditions of future human beings. The power is in the future, so is the responsibility.
comparators.synthesis: Long-term climate trends are understood from a broad sample, but not directly from one village flood or season of a year. Spatial planning combines both broad science and local geography.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Modernity, science and responsibility · Chapter 64

comparators.name: Ch. 65: Multi-Pramāṇa Rationalism
comparators.question: Multi-Pramāṇa Rationalism
comparators.method: The first basic tenet of the parallel philosophy proposed in this text is that of multidimensional rationalism. This does not mean that all evidence is the same or that all beliefs can be true. It means that there is truth and knowledge is possible, but knowledge is not the only kind of evidence. Direct estimates, reliable statements, documents, historical sources, scientific experiments, self-experience, statistical data,…
comparators.purvapaksha: Multidimensionality does not become relativism after all
comparators.uttarapaksha: No, because the types of evidence are considered to be numerous and the standard of truth is not exhaustive. Each claim must bear reasonable area proof, rationale, counterarguments, and amendments. The formula is: Accept plurality of evidence, not chaos of evidence.
comparators.synthesis: Given that there are two opposing views, giving them equal time may be fair, but the false equilibrium arises when the evidence is highly disparate. The existence of a minority opinion is not its scientific weight.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 65

comparators.name: Ch. 66: Coexistential Realism
comparators.question: Coexistential Realism
comparators.method: Another theory is that of coexistential realism. It starts with a rejection of the two extremes. Firstly, the world is only a construction of our consciousness or language; secondly, reality is only a lifeless mass of separate objects and not of any fundamental importance to relationships. Parallel philosophy says that the universe resists, independent of our will, but we always experience it through relationships, body…
comparators.purvapaksha: Assuming a relationship would undermine objective truth
comparators.uttarapaksha: Related to knowledge and object resistance.
comparators.synthesis: The knower is related.Truth is not just a desire for connection. My description may be influenced by language and perspective, but Jagat thwarts the misrepresentation. Medicine, engineering, agriculture, and history define the limits of true resistance in science. Relativism, therefore, refers to a state of knowledge and not to the arbitrariness of truth.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 66

comparators.name: Ch. 67: Dignity-Based Ethics
comparators.question: Dignity-Based Ethics
comparators.method: The moral center of Parallel Philosophy is dignity. Dignity means that the basic moral values of every human being precede birth, caste, sex, wealth, language, religion, ability, position, utility or acceptance by the majority. Man cannot be seen merely as a carrier of means, numbers, labour power, voters, consumers or community prestige.
comparators.purvapaksha: Dignity is a very abstract word
comparators.uttarapaksha: Turn Dignity into a Testable Moral Question
comparators.synthesis: Dignity is not just a sentimental word, so in this chapter, it is governed by four criteria: suffering, autonomy, equal status, and fair distribution. If a practice consistently fails in all four of these, its moral justification is seriously undermined.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 67

comparators.name: Ch. 68: Polycentric Democracy
comparators.question: Polycentric Democracy
comparators.method: Democracy cannot be abolished by elections alone, nor by the institution of parliament or capital. The political doctrine of the Parallel Philosophy is multicentric democracy. This implies a possible decentralization of power, knowledge, resources, and decision-making but equal constitutional protection of fundamental rights.
comparators.purvapaksha: 68.7 PrevParty: Without a strong center, the system will break down
comparators.uttarapaksha: Multicentricity is not fragmentation; it is layered responsibility.
comparators.synthesis: Subjects such as national defence, currency, comprehensive rights-security, and interstate co-ordination may ask for centres; local water, school culture or town-planning may ask for local roles. The doctrine is not anti-centrism but unnecessary anti-centrism.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 68

comparators.name: Ch. 69: The Rational Plurality of Religion
comparators.question: The Rational Plurality of Religion
comparators.method: Parallel theology does not regard atheism as a moral vacuum, nor does it equate faith with superstition. Prudential pluralism means that different religious and non-religious views of life coexist with equal civic dignity, but the test of common propriety applies to public obligations.
comparators.purvapaksha: 69.16 PrevParty: Public Reason itself is the language of the majority
comparators.uttarapaksha: Truth-telling and civil rights are different levels
comparators.synthesis: I can disagree, argue, and change my beliefs about religious truths. However, the basis of civil rights should not depend on a decision about which religion is true. This division allows for truth-telling to survive and limits political repression.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 69

comparators.name: Ch. 70: A Parallel View of History
comparators.question: A Parallel View of History
comparators.method: History is not just a record of the victors. But simply telling the story of the hysteria does not make the story true. The purpose of the parallel historiography is not to create a new myth by reversing the main story; it is to widen the scope, identify silences, and apply the same critical criteria to all claims.
comparators.purvapaksha: Parallel History Will Destroy Objectivity
comparators.uttarapaksha: Parallelism Expands the Field of Evidence
comparators.synthesis: If adding new sources changes the old conclusion, it is not a defeat of objectivity but an improvement. Objectivity is not the absence of a point of view but rather the availability of diverse sources, clear methods, and critical examination and revision.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 70

comparators.name: Ch. 71: The Aphorisms of Parallel Philosophy
comparators.question: The Aphorisms of Parallel Philosophy
comparators.method: To condense the long discourse of this text into thirty aphorisms is not an abstraction but the very essence of the philosophical discipline. The purpose of a sutra is not to make complex ideas into slogans but to provide mnemonic scales with which the reader can examine new questions, controversies, and the institution 's traditions and experiences. Each sutra is an independent sentence, but together they form an…
comparators.purvapaksha: The Thirty Precepts do not constitute a strict code of ethics.
comparators.uttarapaksha: The thread is not a judgment, it is a question.
comparators.synthesis: These formulas are used to guide the question rather than to provide a ready answer. Technical competence may not be morally permissible, but whether a particular technique is appropriate may require separate evidence, risk, benefits, and rights analysis. Birth does not confer moral merit but does require additional arguments on the proper form of social policy. So the thread…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 71

comparators.name: Ch. 72: Epilogue
comparators.question: Epilogue
comparators.method: Parallelism is not just about opposing the mainstream. In parallel, the text contains more method names than place names. It refers to the intellectual state where established knowledge is respectfully examined, neglected sources are discovered, the same critical criteria apply to both, and the conclusions themselves are open to revision.
comparators.purvapaksha: Wouldn 't such open-mindedness be without judgment?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Openness and Moral Boundaries Are Simultaneously Possible
comparators.synthesis: Modification does not have to make everything uncertain. Some moral boundaries may be clear enough: birth is not a moral qualification. a person is not just a means. unnecessary suffering is not appropriate. the state is not the master of the citizen. religious freedom is also a freedom of conscience. majority is not proof of truth. technical competence is not a moral…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Parallel Philosophy: constructive theses · Chapter 72

comparators.name: 1.1 Philosophy: From Wonder to Discernment
comparators.question: How does “1.1 Philosophy: From Wonder to Discernment” develop the chapter's inquiry?
comparators.method: The greatest narrowing of philosophy would be to regard it merely as a history of the views of great philosophers. Philosophy is fundamentally the self-aware intellectual activity through which human beings ask for the reasons behind their beliefs, experiences, values, practices, and institutions. Philosophy brings into question what ordinary life treats as self-evident. “This is true”—why? “This is right”—by what standard?…
comparators.purvapaksha: Philosophy is only the history of ideas
comparators.uttarapaksha: A Critical Dialogue with History
comparators.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not discard history; it communicates the present on the basis of history. Don 't force the thinker of the past into the current vocabulary but examine the present relevance of their question. Philosophy thus becomes the junction of history and living reason.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 1 · indexed section

Don 't force the thinker of the past into the current vocabulary but examine the present relevance of their question. Philosophy thus becomes the junction of history and living reason.
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 1 · indexed section

comparators.name: 1.9 The Initial Promises of the Parallel Philosophy
comparators.question: How does “1.9 The Initial Promises of the Parallel Philosophy” develop the chapter's inquiry?
comparators.method: The greatest narrowing of philosophy would be to regard it merely as a history of the views of great philosophers. Philosophy is fundamentally the self-aware intellectual activity through which human beings ask for the reasons behind their beliefs, experiences, values, practices, and institutions. Philosophy brings into question what ordinary life treats as self-evident. “This is true”—why? “This is right”—by what standard?…

comparators.purvapaksha: How All Evidence Will Finally Be Proven
comparators.uttarapaksha: The Beginning of Error Checking

Common-sense procedures can be given preliminary authority unless there is reasonable resistance; when opposed, mutual testing, independent evidence, and practical success are used to modify the belief through rationalization and source testing. comparators.method: They are true in their own right; their sentences seem attractive to express tolerance, but philosophically call for caution. But this hard fact does not even lead to the conclusion that every reality ends up in only one description. A…

comparators.name: 6.1 The Rigvedic Question: Not a Definitive Story of Creation
comparators.question: How does “6.1 The Rigvedic Question: Not a Definitive Story of Creation” develop the chapter's inquiry?
comparators.method: It is not appropriate to read the earliest background of Indian philosophy as the history of a ready-made theory. In Vedic literature, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanishads, the rituals, deities, world-creation, speech, death, the soul, karma, knowledge, and liberation communicate with and sometimes oppose each other in multiple voices. From this plural world arises the question of later systematic philosophies.
comparators.purvapaksha: 6.16 Purvapaksha: Are the Upanishads only spiritual poems?
comparators.uttarapaksha: Forms of philosophy are not just formulaic arguments. The Upanishads systematically question the limits of existence, knowledge, the self, death, reason, value, and language; they develop arguments through dialogue and example. However, it is also wrong to make every poetic sentence a complete metaphysical theory. Philosophical reconstruction must respect the literary nature of the sources.
comparators.synthesis: Parallel to the Vedic-Upanishadic world, philosophy accepts four basic teachings. First, doubts and questions are also possible within a religious tradition. Secondly, the meaning of external rituals may be reinterpreted by internal experience. Third, multiple answers can coexist in the same tradition. Fourth, acknowledging the limits of knowledge and not abandoning it leads…
comparators.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Indian philosophical traditions · Chapter 6 · indexed section

debates.objection: Philosophy is only the history of ideas
debates.proof: The greatest narrowing of philosophy would be to regard it merely as a history of the views of great philosophers. Philosophy is fundamentally the self-aware intellectual activity through which human beings ask for the reasons behind their beliefs, experiences, values, practices, and institutions. Philosophy brings into question what ordinary life treats as self-evident. “This is true”—why? “This is right”—by what standard?…
debates.response: A Critical Dialogue with History
debates.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not discard history; it communicates the present on the basis of history. Don 't force the thinker of the past into the current vocabulary but examine the present relevance of their question. Philosophy thus becomes the junction of history and living reason.
debates.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 1

debates.objection: How All Evidence Will Finally Be Proven
debates.proof: Doubt is not the enemy of knowledge. disciplined doubt is the keeper of knowledge. But unfounded and equal degrees of infinite doubt about everything is not the ideal of knowledge. If we completely distrust direct perception, memory, linguistic reasoning, and our own reasoning and all shared experiences at the same time, not only philosophy but general behavior will be impossible. The basic question, therefore, is whether or…
debates.response: The Beginning of Error Checking
debates.synthesis: Parallel philosophy does not seek absolute, external, or omniscient evidence. Common-sense procedures can be given preliminary authority unless there is reasonable resistance; when opposed, mutual testing, independent evidence, and practical success are used to modify the belief through rationalization and source testing. This is not infallibility, but error correctionism.
debates.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 2

debates.objection: To say that truth is multifaceted would not lead to relativism.
debates.proof: They are true in their own right; their sentences seem attractive to express tolerance, but philosophically call for caution. If two people say the same thing at the same time, in the same sense, the opposite is true: the lamp is burning and the lamp is not burning; both statements cannot be true in the same sense. But this hard fact does not even lead to the conclusion that every reality ends up in only one description. A…
debates.response: Vision Multipleity Criteria Shared
debates.synthesis: Parallel philosophy says that there can be many perspectives, but each claim must endure sound reason, internal consistency, and the resistance of available evidence, opposition, and experience. Separate statements can be complementary; the question of a decision between diametrically opposed statements cannot be avoided.
debates.source: Gajendra Thakur's Parallel Philosophy · Method and epistemology · Chapter 3

debates.objection: What is the strongest objection or rival explanation that this inquiry must face?
debates.proof: We all know that the person who says this is not knowledge speaks the language of arrogance. Human knowledge is limited, cognitive is limited, memory is flawed, attention is selective, language is incomplete, concepts are historical, institutions may be biased, and everyone 's experience is limited. However, this limitation does not imply that knowledge is impossible. The basic tenet of Parallel Philosophy is that knowledge…
